item.title: Want to Have More Sex? Here's How
item.description:
Low Sexual Desire

Want to Have More Sex? Here's How

Stop waiting until you're in the mood, and cultivate responsive desire.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • Responsive desire is the key to more frequent sex.
  • Waiting to be “in the mood” can keep long-term couples stuck in a low-sex or sexless relationship.
  • Scheduled sensuality can be a bridge back to a renewed sexual life.
Source: (C) Dr Cheryl Fraser

This post is part 4 of a series.

If you want to never have sex again, here's how: Wait until you spontaneously feel horny or turned on.

Wait, what?

Yes, I know that is a little tongue-in-cheek, but I am also serious. Many long-term couples assume they should only make love when desire arrives first. They remember those delicious early days when one kiss could lead to ripping each other’s clothes off, and they assume that is how desire is supposed to work forever.

This type of desire, which sex therapists call spontaneous desire, is often easy to feel in the beginning of a relationship. But over time, spontaneous desire often becomes less frequent. Before you know it, nobody initiates eroticism, weeks turn into months, and before long, the sexual relationship has nearly disappeared. In fact, up to 35 percent of longer-term couples I have interviewed (over 40,000 of them) are not making love at all. I talk about the desire problem in this video.

The Problem With Waiting for Spontaneous Desire

There are different ways clinicians define low-sex and sexless relationships, but in my own work and surveys with thousands of couples, I have seen how common it is for long-term partners to go months, or even years, without making love.

I once worked with a couple who had stopped making love in their 40s and joined my Become Passion online couples program in their 70s. For decades, they had even changed clothes separately so they would not see each other naked. After working on their relationship using my "three keys to passion" model (see the previous two blog posts for a deeper examination of the first two keys—communication and thrill) and their sensual connection, they started making love again. They even walk around the house naked and slap each other’s naked bum. What a beautiful transformation.

Their story is an important reminder that at any age, and even after many years without sex, there is still hope for rebuilding a sensual connection.

Spontaneous Desire Is Only One Kind of Desire

Spontaneous desire is the kind most of us recognize because it seems obvious that we want to feel turned on and sexually motivated before we reach for our sweetheart. I mean, why would we bother to make love if we are not in the mood?

When I first started dating my husband, spontaneous desire was everywhere. We sometimes made love twice a day and even set an alarm for 4:30 in the morning so we could have a quickie before he left for work. Back then, one kiss could wake my sexuality right up. Then I hit menopause, and my lifelong high level of spontaneous desire dried up.

Oh, my friends, I miss it. Yet this is common for both men and women.

Relationships change over time, and so do our bodies, hormones, responsibilities, and energy levels. For many long-term couples, spontaneous desire simply becomes less reliable, and if you keep waiting for it to magically appear, you may end up waiting a very long time for a sensual encounter with your partner.

Meet Responsive Desire

There is a second type of sexual desire. Responsive desire works differently because you need to do something to create desire—you guessed it—in response to a choice. So, you do not necessarily wait to feel in the mood before you begin making moves toward making love. Instead, you may start from what researcher Rosemary Basson describes as sexual neutrality, which simply means you are not turned on yet.

You might decide to begin a sensual encounter because you value your sexual connection, because you usually enjoy yourself once you get going, because it helps you feel closer, or simply because it has been a while and you know it is good for you, your partner, and your relationship. Then, as you start kissing, touching, or cuddling, your mind becomes interested, your body begins to respond, and pleasure has a chance to build.

With responsive desire, desire arises after you begin connecting, rather than being the driving force toward connecting. (For more information on responsive desire, join me for a live online couples workshop on the three keys to passion.)

Yes, I Want You to Schedule Sex

Here comes the advice that many people do not love: Schedule sex.

I understand why that can sound unromantic. You want passion to be spontaneous, and so do I. When spontaneous desire shows up, enjoy the hell out of it. But if you want a consistent erotic relationship, you may need to stop expecting desire to magically arrive before you take any sensual action.

If intercourse feels like too big a leap right now, do not begin there. Schedule other types of pleasurable sensuality instead. You might cuddle naked, spoon in bed, stroke each other’s backs, give a foot rub, or take a shower or bath together. The goal is not to convince yourself into sex, but rather to create opportunities for your body and mind to rediscover touch, pleasure, and connection. So you practice creating, not waiting for, the turn-on.

Think of Sex Like Going to the Gym

I often compare responsive desire to going to the gym. I don’t know about you, but I can guess most of you almost never wake up and feel excited about the gym or lifting weights. So, why do we go to the gym? We go because we know it is good for us and because we know we will usually feel better afterward—and glad we made the effort. We rarely leave an exercise session thinking, “I really wish I hadn’t worked out.”

Sex can sometimes work in a similar way. You may begin by thinking, I’m not really in the mood, but once you start touching, your body may respond, and your mind may become more interested. Afterwards, you might find yourself thinking, I’m really glad we did that.

Scheduled sex may not sound especially sexy at first, but waiting forever for spontaneous desire is not doing your erotic relationship any favors, either. Instead of waiting for desire to rescue your sex life, give responsive desire a place to begin.

So tonight, invite your sweetheart to join you in the shower. Soap each other's bodies, allow the stressors of the day to dissolve down the drain, and invite responsive desire to help you create a satisfying sexual encounter. Just like all three keys to passion, sensuality needs some effort. It is truly worth it.

item.title: We're Asking Sexual Trauma Survivors the Wrong Questions
item.description:
Trauma

We're Asking Sexual Trauma Survivors the Wrong Questions

Some survivors don't understand what happened until years later.

Posted October 8, 2026

Key points
  • Questions people often ask sexual trauma survivors can add to their pain and make them feel responsible.
  • Understanding sexual assault and abuse may take time, especially if the perpetrator was once trusted.
  • Instead of asking why a survivor stayed silent, a better question is: What made it so hard for them to speak?
Source: Tinnakorn jorrunang / Shutterstock

Lately, I’ve been thinking about the ongoing conversations about sexual assault and the expectations people have for survivors after trauma. When a case becomes public, it often elicits differing opinions and misconceptions about what survivors experience and how they cope afterward.

As someone who survived childhood sexual abuse, I understand how these misconceptions can affect healing. When a survivor speaks up about sexual assault or childhood abuse, we often hear questions that make us feel like we are to blame, such as:

Why didn’t you tell someone?

Why did you keep talking to the person who hurt you?

Why didn’t you leave or fight back?

Although I heard these questions firsthand, I didn’t fully realize how harmful they can be until I started my clinical training working with trauma survivors. These questions come up not only in conversations about survivors but also from survivors themselves.

Many people may not realize how much these questions can hurt, so we need to be mindful of how we speak to a survivor, because even if we don’t mean to, our questions can make them feel blamed. It takes extreme courage for survivors to talk about something they may have carried for years, and the last thing they need is to feel like they have to defend themselves.

Instead of asking, “Why didn't they come forward sooner?” we should ask, “What made it so hard for them to tell?”

Sarah’s Story

Sarah is not a real person. Her story is based on a combination of real clinical experiences.

Sarah was drinking with friends when someone she had known and trusted for years sexually assaulted her. She struggled to understand what happened, especially since she never thought this person would hurt her.

After the assault, Sarah began to blame herself and wondered: If I hadn’t been drinking, could I have stopped it? She kept thinking about it and began to believe no one would believe her if she spoke up. Whenever she thought about telling someone, she felt so anxious that she had a panic attack. Her fear kept her silent.

Sarah tried to keep up with her usual routine, going to work and seeing friends. When she attended a social event where her attacker was present, she did her best to act like nothing was wrong and to pretend she was fine. She described these moments as “walking into a room feeling dead inside but knowing that if I did not act normal, everyone would know I felt shattered inside.”

Recent news of a public sexual assault has raised a question that many may have asked Sarah as well: “Why did she keep talking to him?” But that question misses what was happening beneath the surface.

Sarah’s actions don’t mean the assault didn’t happen. They show she was confused and worried about being rejected. For her, pretending everything was normal felt easier than facing all her fears at once.

When Sarah finally told a friend in her social group what happened, her worst fear came true. The friend didn't believe her. Sarah said the hardest part of telling her story was not just being doubted, but also hearing what her friends said when they found out: “It wasn’t rape. I think she regrets sleeping with him.”

These words minimized her experience and left Sarah feeling misunderstood and alone. Eventually, Sarah cut off contact with this mutual friend group. Sarah continued to have nightmares, anxiety, and panic attacks. She started to avoid relationships and found it hard to trust anyone, including her therapist.

Sarah’s story is just one example of how survivors often face hurtful questions and doubt.

This makes me wonder if we're asking survivors the wrong questions. Rather than asking why someone stayed silent or how they managed afterward, we could ask what made it hard for them to speak up in the first place.

For many survivors like Sarah, fear, shame, self-blame, confusion, and fear of not being believed can all play a role in not disclosing abuse.1

When Understanding Comes Years Later

When children experience sexual abuse, they may not fully understand what is happening, which can make it harder for them to talk about it. Even if they know they do not want what is happening and feel scared and confused, they may not have the words or life experience to realize it is abuse.2

When I was abused, it was by someone I knew and trusted. I depended on the adults around me to show me what was safe and what wasn’t. So, when someone I trusted hurt me, I couldn’t understand why they made me feel unsafe in my own body.

My story is not uncommon. Childhood sexual abuse survivors often struggle to make sense of why they were put in unsafe situations and hurt by people they depended on.4 It is hard to make sense of something that shouldn’t happen, so survivors often stay silent out of fear or because they don't know what will happen if they speak up.

When I finally told my story as an adult, the first thing I was asked was, “Why didn’t you tell someone?” That might sound like a fair question, but it made me feel as though they were questioning me since I had not disclosed the abuse sooner. The real issue was that I needed years to process it and learn that I didn't deserve what happened to me.

Similarly, I have worked with adult survivors who told me that even though they remembered what happened, they could not make sense of their feelings as children until they accepted it was abuse.3 Coming to this understanding can be long and painful.

People naturally offer children understanding because they know children are never to blame. We should give sexual assault survivors the same understanding. This starts with how we speak to them, the questions we ask, and the time we give them to process their experience.

Survivors don't need more questions that make them defend themselves. They need questions that help us understand what they lived through. Maybe it is time to stop asking survivors why they didn't come forward sooner, and start asking what made it so hard to come forward in the first place.
